description: We are a multidisciplinary team of four: one Applied and Computational Mathematics student, one Software Engineering student, one Control and Automation Engineering student and one Law student. Together we combine mathematical modeling, data analysis, software development, systems thinking and a legal and social perspective. We love turning complex data into tools that help people. We welcome anyone who wants to learn, with skills in design, UX/UI, communication or Earth science.
summary: ForeCast is a web platform that turns NASA Earth observation data into a clear picture of rainfall history and territorial exposure in Southern Brazil (Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul), a region hit by increasingly severe floods, including the 2024 Rio Grande do Sul disaster. We processed 288 months of NASA GPM IMERG precipitation (2001–2024) and GLDAS soil moisture data into an interactive map. Users can play the rainfall month by month, compare each month with its own historical average, and inspect any of 5,458 grid cells through charts and tables. Regional views add extreme-rainfall indicators and statistical trend results. They also add exploratory layers that combine highways (OpenStreetMap) and terrain (NASADEM) to point out road segments worth investigating. Scientific climate data is usually scattered and hard to read. ForeCast makes it understandable for citizens, civil defense teams and researchers, and it is open about its sources and limitations. It is the first step toward a preparedness tool that will connect climate history, weather forecasts, alerts and confirmed shelters to support emergency route planning.
details:
What it does and how it works

ForeCast has three connected views:

  • Climate Dossier: an animated map of monthly rainfall from January 2001 to December 2024, covering 5,458 NASA IMERG cells at 0.1°. Users can play, pause, change speed or jump to any month. They can switch between total rainfall (mm) and percentage anomaly. The anomaly compares each month with the average of that same calendar month for that same cell, so normal seasonal variation is not mistaken for an extreme. Selecting a cell opens its full 288-month chart and table.
  • Native Grid Explorer: lets users browse NASA products at their original resolution: IMERG at 0.1° and GLDAS Noah soil moisture at 0.25°. No interpolation is used to fake a higher resolution.
  • Regional Investigation: shows regional indicators such as annual precipitation, maximum one-day rainfall (RX1DAY), days with 50 mm or more of rain (R50MM) and surface soil moisture. It also shows trend tests corrected for multiple comparisons, plus exploratory layers for highways, terrain and candidate crossing points.

The architecture separates science from serving. Python scripts download, check (SHA-256 checksums, units, coordinates) and process NASA NetCDF files into versioned JSON/GeoJSON derived files with provenance. A FastAPI backend serves these files, and a React frontend renders them. A browser request never triggers heavy downloads or statistical processing, so the experience stays fast and the results are reproducible.

Benefits and intended impact

In an extreme rainfall event, the information people need is scattered across scientific datasets, maps, disaster records and local agencies. ForeCast brings the historical and territorial evidence into one visual place. It helps answer two questions: What happened here? and Where should we look more closely?

  • Citizens can understand how rainfall in their region has changed.
  • Municipal and civil defense teams can explore historical patterns and infrastructure exposure to support preparedness.
  • Researchers and students can access transparent series, units, periods and limitations.

In the long term, ForeCast aims to support population safety during extreme events. The plan is to connect official flood records, short-term weather forecasts, operational alerts, road closures and confirmed shelters to help plan emergency routes, always validated with the responsible authorities.

Tools, languages and technologies

  • NASA data: GPM IMERG Final monthly (GPM_3IMERGM, V07) and daily (GPM_3IMERGDF), GLDAS Noah 2.1 monthly soil moisture, and NASADEM elevation.
  • Other data: IBGE state and regional boundaries, and OpenStreetMap road network.
  • Data processing: Python, NumPy, xarray, netCDF4, Shapely and pyproj.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, and an HTML Canvas for the high-performance monthly animation.
  • Testing: pytest and Vitest.
  • Deployment: Render (API) and Cloudflare Pages (frontend), both on free tiers.
  • Languages: the interface is available in Portuguese and English.

How the project is creative

Instead of showing one rainfall chart, ForeCast lets users watch 24 years of rainfall unfold across a whole region, month by month, while following a single location. Comparing each month with its own calendar average shows real anomalies instead of normal seasonal swings. We also combined climate data with terrain and road networks to start linking “where it rains” to “what infrastructure may be affected”. This bridges climate science and practical preparedness.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty: an anomaly is not presented as a flood forecast, and a terrain feature is not presented as a confirmed risk. Modeled GLDAS soil moisture is labeled as a simulation, not a measurement. Limitations are documented and shown to users.
  • Data quality: missing values are never turned into zero, and real zeros are kept. Fill values and invalid values are handled explicitly. Anomalies are published only when all 24 years are valid.
  • Reproducibility: checksums, provenance and versioned outputs make it possible to trace and rebuild every result.
  • Performance: data is pre-processed and split into yearly blocks, with caching and prefetching, so the animation runs smoothly even on modest devices.
  • Accessibility and reach: the interface is bilingual, uses fixed color scales so months can be compared, and is free to host so it stays sustainable.
  • Responsibility: the prototype does not replace official alerts. Any future evacuation-routing feature will require operational data and validation with civil defense agencies.
